To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a subset of brainstem neurons respond preferentially to vestibular exafference, 2) this exafference is normally canceled in active movement by a mechanism located in the cerebel- lum and 3) the resulting “sensory con- flict” may be a key component of motion sickness etiology, and could be used to develop more effective prevention and treatment.

“A subset of brainstem and cerebeller neurons responds preferentially to passive, rather than self-initiated head movements, and these neurons are likely involved in the generation of motion sickness.”

the vestibular nuclei contain neurons that respond preferentially when the head is moved passively, and these neurons are activated during passive movement when the vestibular organs are stimulated by the environment, but not by self-generated movement, suggesting that they may play a role in motion sickness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neural mechanisms of motion sickness.
the brain mechanisms of motion sickness and the development of effective treatments for this common and debilitating condition.
the role of the vestibular system in the control of posture and locomotion and the etiology of motion sickness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“the origin of motion sickness remains elusive.”
the brainstem processing of vestibulocollic reflex is the most plausible explanation for the origin of motion sickness.
“motion sickness is caused by a sensory conflict between the vestibular system and the visual and/or tactile system.”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
motion sickness is caused by a mismatch in the vestibular system.

motion sickness may be caused by a persistent “internal sensory conflict,” resulting in persistent activation of emetic brainstem centers, and that the “sensory” aspect of this conflict is mediated by a class of brainstem neurons responding to vestibular “exafference.”
the brainstem processing of vestibulo-spinal reflexes, and the associated cerebellar processing, is the key to motion sickness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brainstem is the most likely site of the “sensory mismatch” that causes motion sickness.
a subset of neurons in the brainstem and cerebella are responsible for motion sickness.

there exists a class of brainstem vestibular neurons that respond preferentially when the vestibular system receives exafferent sensory input during passive head movements, but not during active movements.
